title: Abbott Elementary
synopsis: There are eleven glue sticks for forty kids and someone unplugged the laminator. It's only Tuesday.

nodes.text: The supply closet contains: one ream of pink paper, a stapler with no staples, a laminating pouch somebody already used, and a single dehydrated googly eye. You stand there a beat too long. Behind you the crew does the thing where they slowly push in on your face, and you do the thing where you pretend not to know they're doing it.

choices.consequence: You draft it three times. The final version contains the word 'circling' and you hate yourself a little for it. You email Ava politely. It gets you to Ava's Reply, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

Forty kids, one color, zero budget. You have made worse ideas work with less than this. You commit to improvise pink-paper week. The road to Ava's Reply is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Twenty minutes later: three emojis and a GIF. No supplies, no budget code, no acknowledgment that a request was made by a human being. You can hear the espresso machine from the hallway — the one expensed as 'faculty wellness infrastructure' — grinding away behind a closed door with a neon sign on it.

choices.consequence: You look directly into the camera. You don't say anything. You don't have to say anything. You choose to note the espresso. By Mr. Howard's Room, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

choices.text: Ask for the budget code anyway
choices.consequence: You send a second email, sunnier than the first. She replies with a fourth emoji. Progress is progress. You ask for the budget code anyway. It gets you to Mr. Howard's Room, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: An unopened twelve-pack of construction paper is sitting on Mr. Howard's back counter like it's daring you. It is 7:51. He does not get in until 8:10, and in thirty years he has never used construction paper for anything except a bulletin board about himself.

choices.text: Take one pack, leave a note
choices.consequence: You write BORROWED — J.T. on a Post-it. You will spend the next six hours composing the follow-up conversation in your head. You choose to take one pack, leave a note. By Barbara, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You take the entire twelve-pack. You are a thief in a cardigan and the camera got every second of it. You take it all. It gets you to Barbara, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Barbara does not give you twenty-two markers. Barbara sets a box down on the corner of your desk while discussing something else entirely, does not look at the box, does not look at you, and continues out the door mid-sentence. The box contains twenty-two markers. All of them work. She tested them.

choices.consequence: You say it low, to her back. She raises one hand without turning around. That is the whole exchange. That is how it works. You thank her quietly. It gets you to Janine, You, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.
You call her a softie in front of Melissa and she says she has no idea what you're referring to, then takes the box back for eleven seconds.

nodes.text: There's a moment in the hall where you catch your own reflection in the laminator glass — pink paper under one arm, marker box under the other, hair attempting something ambitious — and the reflection says, in your voice, 'You got this.' You have started giving yourself pep talks in the third person. The crew is absolutely filming this.

choices.consequence: You do, actually. About nine percent of the time. Today is a nine percent day and you are going to ride it. You believe yourself. It gets you to Jacob, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You roll them so hard you nearly drop the markers, and then keep walking, because you do in fact got this. You roll your eyes. It gets you to Jacob, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: Jacob has a plan and the plan is a TikTok. He has written a script. The script has a hook, a call to action, and a section explaining public school funding through a metaphor involving a birthday party. He wants to shoot it in the hallway. He has a ring light in his car. He brought the ring light on purpose.

choices.consequence: You say yes with three conditions. He agrees to all three and honors approximately one and a half of them. You choose to approve carefully. By Gregory, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You cut the birthday party metaphor. He calls it 'a big swing.' It was a big swing. It was also four minutes long. You edit the script first. It gets you to Gregory, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: The laminator, dead since Thursday, is on. Gregory is walking away from it with a screwdriver in his back pocket and a face fully committed to having had nothing to do with anything. He does not mention it. He will never mention it. He fixed a laminator and would like the record to show he was simply passing by.

choices.consequence: You say thank you and he says 'for what' and neither of you moves for a full two seconds. The crew zooms in. You choose to tell him you noticed. By Pink Facts Week, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You say nothing and he says nothing and it is extremely weird, in a good way, for the rest of the afternoon. You commit to don't make it weird. The road to Pink Facts Week is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Twenty minutes into pink paper week, Marcus raises his hand and asks whether pink is a real color or 'just light red.' Thirty-nine seven-year-olds turn around to look at you. You open your mouth. You discover — live, on camera, in front of a child who trusts you completely — that you do not know the answer to this question.

choices.consequence: You write PINK: AN INVESTIGATION on the board in enormous letters and buy yourself a week. It becomes the best unit you teach all year. You commit to make it a project. The road to Melissa is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You say 'I don't know — let's find out,' which is the correct pedagogical response and also a stall, and both of those are true at once. You commit to admit you don't know. The road to Melissa is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Melissa comes in without knocking, sets a box of bandages on the corner of your desk, says 'just in case,' and leaves. She does not specify in case of what. Ten minutes later you hear a sound from the hallway that you would have to describe as a thud with intent behind it.

choices.consequence: You take the bandages. You will use eleven of them before Thursday. You will never ask how she knew. You take it. It gets you to Lunch, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You call after her asking which kid. She says 'you'll know,' from around the corner, already gone. You joke about which kid. It gets you to Lunch, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: You eat at your desk: a granola bar, half a cold coffee, eight minutes. The crew has mercifully gone to film the cafeteria, where something is unfolding involving chocolate milk and a moral principle. For eight entire minutes, nobody is looking at you. You had forgotten what that is like.

choices.consequence: You get through half of Wednesday before the bell. It's a good half. It is genuinely a good half. You choose to read tomorrow's plan. By Mr. Johnson, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You put your head back and close your eyes for six of the eight minutes, and it is the single most productive thing you do all day. You choose to just breathe. By Mr. Johnson, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Mr. Johnson leans in the doorway holding a mop he is not using and tells you, very calmly, that the laminator cord did not fall out. It was removed. Wound up. Placed on a shelf. 'Someone,' he says, 'made a decision.' Then he tells you an unrelated story about a raccoon which he clearly considers highly relevant.

choices.consequence: You spend fifteen minutes of prep doing detective work in an elementary school. You find nothing. You have never been more certain of anything in your life.

You let it go. Mr. Johnson nods slowly, in a manner suggesting he knows exactly who did it and is choosing peace. You choose to let it go. By Ava, Again, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Ava appears with an iPad and an announcement: she has a plan for the supply shortage. The plan is a raffle. There are tiers. There is a tier called Principal's Circle. She has already made the flyer, and the flyer has her face on it, and her face is larger than the name of the school.

choices.consequence: You tell her the flyer is eye-catching, which is true, and she receives it as a full endorsement, which it was not. You choose to indulge her. By Mom Call, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

You suggest the prizes could maybe be things rather than experiences with her. She writes it down. She does not change it. You commit to push back kindly. The road to Mom Call is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Marcus's mom calls at 1:40, during your one free block. You brace. Instead she tells you Marcus came home and talked about pink for forty-five straight minutes, made her look at a paint chip, and has not voluntarily discussed school since the first grade. Then she goes quiet and says thank you in a way that undoes you slightly.

choices.consequence: You ask her to come talk to the class about anything she likes. She picks nursing. It is the best Friday of the semester. You invite her in. It gets you to Crisis, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You tell her Wednesday is about why the sky isn't pink. She laughs. You now have to actually go and teach that. You promise next week's theme. It gets you to Crisis, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: A tearful aide appears in your doorway. There has been a glue stick situation in K-2. She will not elaborate on the word 'situation,' and you get the strong sense that elaborating would make it considerably worse. From down the hall comes a sound like twelve small people all deciding something at exactly the same time.

choices.consequence: You go down, you kneel, you use the voice. Eleven minutes and one confiscated glue stick later there is peace in K-2. You resolve it sweetly. It gets you to Howard's Quiet Apology, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You fetch Howard, who does not want to help, and who then resolves it in ninety seconds because he is — infuriatingly — very good at this. You recruit Mr. Howard. It gets you to Howard's Quiet Apology, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: At 2:15 Mr. Howard walks into your room carrying a fresh ream of paper, sets it on the counter, and says, 'They had extra.' They did not have extra. He bought this. He is now examining your word wall with tremendous professional interest so that he does not have to be looked at directly.

choices.consequence: You say thank you and he says 'for what' and immediately begins critiquing your word wall, which is his love language. You commit to thank him. The road to Faculty Lounge is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You let him off the hook entirely, and he stands there one second longer than he needs to before he goes. You smile and move on. It gets you to Faculty Lounge, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

nodes.text: The coffee is objectively terrible — it has been on the burner since six and has entered a new state of matter. But Barbara is telling a story about 1997, and Melissa is disputing key details of it, and Jacob is taking the whole thing extremely seriously, and Gregory is laughing without producing any sound. Nobody wants to leave.

choices.consequence: You let all of it out — the closet, the emojis, the cord — and four people say 'mm' at precisely the right moments and you feel eighty percent better.

choices.text: Pivot to a plan for next week
choices.consequence: You grab a napkin and start writing, and by the end of the period four teachers have signed on to a color of the week. You choose to pivot to a plan for next week. By After School, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Marcus stays behind and hands you a notebook. Inside: eighteen shades of pink, hand-mixed, each one labeled in careful seven-year-old handwriting. 'Sunset.' 'Inside of a shell.' 'Gum after.' You look at page four for a long moment and have to make a decision about your face, because the camera is right there.

choices.consequence: You buy a frame at CVS that costs more than you'd like and hang page four by the door where every kid walks past it. You frame it. It gets you to Crew Interview, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You pin the notebook open on the corkboard and turn to a new page every morning. He checks. Every single morning, he checks. You choose to keep it on the corkboard. By Crew Interview, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: They sit you down in the empty classroom with the light coming gold through the blinds and ask the question they ask every day: 'So — how was today?' You have eleven glue sticks, forty kids, a principal running a raffle with her own face on the flyer, and a notebook full of pink in your bag.

choices.consequence: You say it was hard. You say a lot of the time it's hard. Then you say the other thing, and the crew does not cut away. You commit to honestly. The road to 3:08 p.m. is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.
You say 'good!' with your whole chest, and hold it, and hold it — and then laugh, because they have been filming you for two years and they know.

nodes.text: The bell. The hallway detonates. Four hundred children exit the building at a velocity that should not be structurally possible, and then all at once it stops. You sit down in a room with thirty-nine empty chairs and one pink notebook, and the sound of a floor buffer starting up somewhere very far away.

choices.consequence: You pull out Wednesday and get all the way through it, and it's good, and you are a little surprised by that. You plan tomorrow. It gets you to Home, though not with the dignity or plausible deniability you would have preferred.

You sit for nine more minutes doing absolutely nothing, which you have earned, and which nobody films. You choose to sit a little longer. By Home, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Pasta, wine, and a bath you fully intend to take. You take the bath. You get out. You put on the show. You watch four minutes of the show. Then the laptop comes open 'just to check something,' and at 11:40 you fall asleep sitting up with a curriculum doc on your chest and every light in the apartment still on.

choices.consequence: You close the laptop at 11:41 and are asleep by 11:42. This is the correct answer and you almost never choose it. You commit to sleep. The road to Wednesday is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You send one more email at 12:06 a.m. Ava replies at 12:07 with a thumbs up, which raises several questions about Ava. You choose to one more email. By Wednesday, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

nodes.text: Same closet. Same stapler. Slightly more glue, from a source nobody will identify. The pink paper is nearly gone, and there is a note taped inside the door in handwriting you recognize as Howard's, listing which supply room actually keeps the good scissors. And the googly eye has moved about four inches to the left.

choices.consequence: You do another week of pink, because the kids demand it and because you have paper. Sometimes that is the entire curriculum decision. You commit to pink, again. The road to Pink Facts Forever is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

You write BLUE on the board and thirty-nine kids groan and then immediately start arguing about which blue, which means it worked. You choose to new color. By Funded, Finally, the plan will either look inspired or become a story told at your expense for years.

There is a version of today that is not about supplies at all, and it has been waiting since 7:42 yesterday morning. You commit to take the third path. The road to Janine, on Tape is now open, and at least two people are already preparing to misunderstand why.

nodes.text: Pink Facts Week becomes a thing. Then it becomes an annual thing. Other teachers steal it outright, which is the highest honor available in this building. Six years later a very tall middle schooler stops you in a Wawa to tell you he still knows why pink isn't on the rainbow — and then, because he is thirteen, becomes instantly embarrassed and leaves. You stand in the chip aisle for a minute.

Ava's raffle raises four thousand two hundred dollars, which nobody can explain, least of all Ava, who maintains she 'always saw the vision.' The supply closet gets restocked for the first time since the Obama administration. At the assembly they hand you the certificate, and you take the mic, and you give the entire thing to her — and for one full second, on camera, Ava Coleman has no comeback.

The documentary airs. People recognize you at CVS and want to talk about the pink episode. Your mother sends the clip to everyone she has ever met, including her dentist. A production company calls. And on Monday you are back in the building at 7:42 with a ream of paper under your arm, because that was never the point. You teach. You teach. You teach.
